text: Once you're working inside a scoped application context in Studio — the context you entered the moment you finished Lesson 20's Create Application wizard — every customization you create from that point forward is automatically organized and tracked under that application's record. A table, a Business Rule, a Client Script, a Script Include, a UI Page: every one is automatically associated with the same application, visible together, with no extra step.

This isn't a folder you have to remember to file things into. It's automatic, structural behavior tied to the fact that you're working inside that application's scope. Everything created while you're in that context belongs to that context.

Compare that to Global scope — exactly the kind of customization this course's earlier chapters had you build, since Chapters 1 through 4 never required a scoped application to exist. A Business Rule in Global, a Client Script in Global, a Script Include in Global: each exists as its own standalone record, with no automatic grouping tying them together as the pieces that make up one logical application.

An instance with years of Global customizations accumulated by different admins has no structural way to answer which of a hundred Business Rules belong together as one coherent thing — you'd reconstruct that grouping by hand, from naming conventions, memory, or documentation that may or may not exist.

This organization isn't just a nicer developer experience. It's exactly what makes an application exportable and packageable as a coherent unit. Because Studio already knows every table, script, and UI artifact that belongs to x_acme_fleet, the platform can treat that whole set as one thing — moving it between instances, publishing it, or sharing it with another team, without someone manually hunting down every piece first.

This course doesn't go deep on packaging mechanics, but the connection matters: the same scope-based organization from Lesson 19 that prevents naming collisions is also what makes an application a well-defined, movable unit. Isolation and packageability are two outcomes of the same underlying structure. Chapter 6 has you build a real data model, and every piece of it will already be organized this way — Studio will already know. Next up: a worked lab scenario applying everything from this chapter.
